cards.a:
der Bug = bow — the front of the boat.
das Heck = stern — the back of the boat.

Backbord = port — the left side when facing the bow.
Steuerbord = starboard — the right side when facing the bow.
Amidships — in the middle of the boat. In a helm command, Ruder mittschiffs! means to centre the rudder.
Ahead — in front of the boat. Fahrt voraus means moving forwards.
Astern — behind the boat. Fahrt achteraus means moving backwards.
Abeam — off either side, at a right angle to the boat's fore-and-aft line.
Aboard / on board — on or into the boat. Komm an Bord! means “Come aboard!”
Hull — the main body of the boat.
Keel — on a typical sailing yacht, the fixed fin beneath the hull that resists sideways drift and usually carries ballast.
Rudder — the underwater steering surface. In commands, Ruder can also refer to the helm; it does not mean the wheel alone.
Tiller — the lever used to turn the rudder.
Steering wheel / wheel — the wheel used to steer the boat.
Waterline — the line where the water surface meets the hull.
Draught (US: draft) — the vertical distance from the waterline to the boat's lowest underwater point.
Freeboard — the vertical distance from the waterline to the deck edge.
Heel / heeling — the boat leaning to one side, for example under wind pressure. The verb is krängen.
Bilge — the lowest internal part of the hull, where water can collect.
Deck — the boat's upper walking surface. An Deck means “on deck”.
Cockpit — the recessed area where the crew usually sits and steers. Also called die Plicht in German.
Companionway — the entrance and steps leading below deck.
Hatch — an opening in the deck or cabin top, usually with a closable cover.
Cockpit locker / seat locker — a storage compartment, often beneath a cockpit seat.

die Reling = guardrail / railing — the barrier along the deck edge; its wires are often called lifelines in US English.
die Relingsstütze = stanchion — an upright post supporting it.
Pulpit / bow rail — the rigid safety rail at the bow.
Pushpit / stern rail — the rigid safety rail at the stern.
Cleat — a fitting with two horns around which a line can be secured.
Mast — the upright spar supporting the sails.
Boom — the spar along the foot of a sail. The mainsail's boom is also called der Großbaum.
Forestay — the standing-rigging wire or rod supporting the mast towards the bow.
Backstay — the standing-rigging wire or rod supporting the mast towards the stern.
Shrouds — the rigging that supports the mast from the sides. Die Wanten is plural; one shroud is die Want.
Halyard — a line used to hoist a sail. Nautical German uses das Fall; the plural is die Fallen.
Sheet — a line used to adjust a sail's angle to the wind.
Mainsheet — the sheet controlling the mainsail, usually through its boom.
Jib sheet — the sheet controlling the jib.
Topping lift — a line from high on the mast to the boom's outer end, used to support the boom.
Boom vang (UK: kicker) — the tackle or strut that restrains the boom from lifting.
Outhaul — the control that pulls the mainsail's clew along the boom to adjust tension in the foot.
Winch — a drum used to gain pulling power when handling a loaded line.
Winch handle — the removable handle used to turn a winch.
Block — a pulley in a housing, used to lead a line or form part of a tackle.
Mainsail — the principal sail set behind the main mast.
Jib — on a typical modern yacht, a headsail that does not overlap the mast.
Genoa — an overlapping headsail, extending aft beyond the mast.
Spinnaker — a large, light sail used mainly with the wind from the side or behind.
Sail batten — a stiff strip fitted into a sail pocket to support the sail's shape.

cards.q: das Vorliek / das Achterliek / das Unterliek
cards.a:
On a triangular sail:
das Vorliek = luff — the leading edge.
das Achterliek = leech — the trailing edge.
das Unterliek = foot — the bottom edge.

cards.q: der Segelkopf / der Hals / das Schothorn
cards.a:
On a triangular sail:
der Segelkopf = head — the top corner.
der Hals = tack — the lower forward corner.
das Schothorn = clew — the lower aft corner.

Luv = windward — towards the side the wind comes from.
Lee = leeward — towards the side away from the wind.
True wind — the wind before accounting for the boat's motion. The wind felt on a moving boat is the apparent wind.
Apparent wind — the wind felt on board a moving boat, combining the true wind with the effect of the boat's motion.
Gust — a brief increase in wind speed. Also written die Böe; the plural is die Böen.
Calm — a period of little or no wind.

cards.q: am Wind / Halbwind / raumschots / vor dem Wind
cards.a:
am Wind = close-hauled / on the wind — sailing towards the wind, as close as the boat can sail efficiently.
Halbwind = beam reach — wind from the side, roughly at right angles to the boat.
raumschots = broad reach — wind from behind the beam.
vor dem Wind = running / dead downwind — wind from directly astern.
Head to wind — the bow points directly into the wind. Ordinary sails cannot drive the boat forwards in this position.
Head up / luff up — turn the bow towards the wind.
Bear away / bear off — turn the bow away from the wind.
Tack / go about — change tack by turning the bow through the wind. Klar zur Wende! means “Ready about!”
Gybe (US: jibe) — change tack by turning the stern through the wind. Klar zur Halse! means “Stand by to gybe!”
Beat to windward — work upwind by sailing successive tacks.
Set / hoist the sails — raise or deploy them for sailing. Großsegel setzen! means “Hoist the mainsail!”
Take in / lower the sails — bring them down or otherwise take them out of use. Bergen is broader than just pulling a sail down.
Reef — reduce the area of sail set. Das Großsegel reffen means “reef the mainsail”.
Haul in / sheet in — pull a line in. Die Schot dichtholen means “sheet in”.
Ease / pay out — let a line out under control. Die Schot fieren means “ease the sheet”.
Line / rope — a length of rope used on board. Lines often have more specific names according to their job.
Bowline — a knot forming a fixed loop. Here, bowline is the knot; a bow line is a mooring line at the bow.
Clove hitch — a hitch around a post or rail, commonly used to attach a fender line.
Figure-of-eight knot — a stopper knot tied near the end of a line.
Coil a line — gather it into orderly loops for stowage.
Mooring line / mooring warp — a line used to secure a boat to a berth or mooring.

die Vorleine = bow line — a mooring line leading forward from the bow.
die Achterleine = stern line — a mooring line leading aft from the stern.

die Vorspring = forward spring / bow spring — leads aft from the forward part of the boat and checks forward movement.
die Achterspring = aft spring / stern spring — leads forward from the aft part of the boat and checks backward movement.

English spring-line names vary; the lead and the movement restrained are the useful distinction.
Fender — a cushion hung between the hull and a quay, pontoon or another boat to prevent contact damage.
Berth / come alongside — bring the boat to a quay, pontoon or other berth.
Leave the berth / cast off — depart from a quay, pontoon or other berth.
Make fast / secure — tie up the boat or secure a line. Die Leine festmachen! means “Make the line fast!”
Anchor — the equipment lowered to the seabed to hold the boat in place.
Anchor chain — the chain connecting the anchor to the boat; some boats use a combination of chain and rope.
Compass — an instrument showing direction relative to north.
Course — the direction the boat is steered or travels, usually expressed in degrees. More precise terms distinguish a steered course from a course over ground.
Nautical mile — a unit of distance equal to 1,852 metres.
Knot — a unit of speed equal to one nautical mile per hour. Knoten can also mean a knot tied in a rope.
Lifejacket — personal flotation equipment designed to support a person in the water. Rettungsweste anlegen! means “Put on your lifejacket!”
Lifebuoy / life ring — a floating ring thrown to someone in the water.
Safety harness — the harness worn to connect a person to the boat using a tether. On modern lifejackets the harness may be integrated.
Man overboard! / Person overboard! — the alarm that someone has fallen into the water. Mensch über Bord! is also used in German.
